newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-BTR in transition, payout plunges.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-BTR in transition, payout plunges.

text.p: New chief executive Ian Strachan on Thursday set out a plan of drastic action at Anglo-Australian diversfied industrials group BTR Plc that is intended to restore earnings growth by closing units and cutting the 1996 dividend.
The transition plan all but wiped out profits for the first half of 1996 due to provisions for reorganisation costs and losses on disposals totalling 622 million pounds ($967 million).
To help pay for the streamlining, and to better reflect its new structure, BTR said it would pay an interim dividend of 4.0 pence per share, down from 5.54 pence for first half 1995.
This would probably be followed by a cut in the final dividend to 5.6 pence from last year's 9.15 pence, it added.
Strachan told Reuters that the board "had decided to rebase the dividend and to adopt a policy of dividend growth from the new base brodly in line with the growth in underlying earnings."
In future, the company will be based around seven business groups, instead of 32 product groups, anchored in automotive and industrial engineering as well as packaging and materials.

"The retained group with (1995-equivalent) sales of 7.0 billion pounds has a return on capital after adding back goodwill of 16.4 percent. This is significantly value-creating as far as shareholders are concerned," Strachan told Reuters.

Including the 182.5 million pound sale of its electric power group, provisionally agreed on Thursday, BTR has completed about two-thirds of its planned divestments and has a range of smaller units with sales equal to about 840 million pounds left to sell.
The biggest tranche of disposals -- including its Taiwanese polymer interests, the U.S. assets of aggregates group Tilcon and the electric power units -- happened in the past 10 days.
Strachan said the 349 million pounds of restructuring items, some 45 percent of which will be in continental Europe, had been planned in detail and would be stuck to rigorously.
"I think it's very difficult in continental Europe to drive through restructuring, but we intend to do that," he said.
He called the programme "very specific and one-off", adding, "It is clearly part of our strategy of growth going forward."

Stripping out the exceptional effects of the restructuring and divestments, BTR's core earnings slipped slightly in the half-year, despite higher sales, due to weakness in its automotive systems units which Strachan said was under control.
Beyond seeking to exit those areas which have been a drag on the business, Strachan said it was important for BTR to seek market leadership from its key future "building block" units.

"The target is not described necessarily in mathematical terms. (It) is to achieve a position in these major global groups as an undisputed leader, (which) means having substantial market share and distinctive competitive advantages."
Already, Strachan noted, many BTR units in areas like process valves, power drives and industrial batteries lead their competitors in market, technology, product or cost terms.
"These are very strong market positions. We're not talking about aspirations that are not found in reality. This is today."
Tactics for the future would include the continued search for bolt-on acquisitions for the growth groups, as well as an ambition to focus heavily on emerging markets.
He said BTR hopes that by 2000, 15 percent of group sales can be from such areas where it sees high growth potential, and opportunities to drive forward new products and manufacturing.
Analysts said the rAdical package was what they had been hoping for to stop the rot of underperformance at the group.
Despite the payout cut, which normally would have triggered disappointment, the company's share price rose as investors welcome Strachan's strong medicine.
By midday the shares had stabilised up 7-1/2 pence at 273.5 pence, in heavy turnover of nearly 22 million shares. ($1=.6430 Pound)
